files.lesson.md: --- order: 11 unit: using node: AC9M8A03 n2 uses: [AC9M7N07 n2, AC9M8N04 n1] # models give negative values (−10 × 12 + 100) that students judge title: Comparing two plans summary: Put two rules on one graph. Where the lines cross they cost the same; on either side, the lower line is the cheaper plan. Then check where the model makes sense. language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Phone plans, gyms and streaming services all ask you to choose between a bigger fee and a lower rate. Two lines on one graph answer it for any amount." connection: gym-or-casual # data/connections/maths.yml app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8139 url: http://127.0.0.1:8139/index.html readySelector: "#sl-k" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: graph.yml#pic, caption: "Plan A ($T = 5g + 20$) and Plan B ($T = 40$) cost the same at 4 GB. Below 4 GB, A is lower (cheaper); above 4 GB, B is." } explainClip: query: { code: "@graph.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Where the lines cross, the plans cost the same" say: "Where the lines cross, the two plans cost the same." clip: - caption: { text: "Plan A: 20 dollars plus 5 per GB. Plan B: one flat price.", say: "Plan A is twenty dollars plus five per gigabyte; Plan B is one flat price." } - caption: { text: "Here B is 30 dollars: the same as A at 2 GB.", say: "Here Plan B is thirty dollars, the same as Plan A at two gigabytes." } - wait: 400 - caption: { text: "Make Plan B 40 dollars: now they cost the same at 4 GB.", say: "Make Plan B forty dollars, and now they cost the same at four gigabytes." } - click: Make k bigger - wait: 400 - caption: { text: "Left of the crossing, Plan A is cheaper; right of it, Plan B is.", say: "Left of the crossing, Plan A is cheaper; to the right, Plan B is." } - wait: 1200 - expect: { selector: "#board", contains: "g = 4" } --- You've written one rule for one situation. Choosing between two plans needs two rules on the same graph, and a question answered in the situation's own words: which plan, for how much data, and does the answer make sense? ## Predict: which plan? ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to a plan before seeing the graph exposes the belief that the lower fee always wins." check: type: predict q: "Plan A costs 20 dollars a month plus 5 dollars per GB. Plan B costs 40 dollars a month for any amount of data. Mia uses 6 GB a month. Which plan is cheaper for her?" options: ["Plan A: it has the lower fee", "Plan B", "They cost the same"] actual: "Plan B. For 6 GB, Plan A costs 20 + 5 × 6 = 50 dollars and Plan B costs 40. A's lower fee only wins for small amounts of data." ``` (The plan prices are made up for the task.) Work out what each plan costs for 6 GB. Then think: is there an amount of data where they cost the same? ## Run: where they cost the same ```step stage: run insight: "On one graph the two plans' lines cross at a single point: the amount of data where they cost the same, which splits the light users from the heavy ones." try: { playground: board, starter: "graph.yml#run", height: 640 } check: { type: board, text: "Drag $P$ to where the two plans cost the same.", when: "P on y = 5x + 20 and P on y = 40" } ``` Plan A is $T = 5g + 20$; Plan B is $T = 40$. Drag $P$ to where the lines cross. Then look at 6 GB: which line is lower there? Was your prediction right? ## Investigate: answering in words ```step stage: investigate insight: "The crossing answers 'when do they cost the same'; the lower line answers 'which is cheaper'; and a model only makes sense for some values." tasks: - picture: { ref: graph.yml#pic, caption: "They cross at $(4, 40)$: 4 GB costs 40 dollars on either plan." } check: type: question q: "For 2 GB a month, which plan is cheaper?" options: ["Plan A", "Plan B", "They cost the same"] answer: 0 explain: "For 2 GB, Plan A costs 20 + 5 × 2 = 30 dollars and Plan B costs 40. Left of the crossing, Plan A's line is lower." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#leo" text: "Leo compares the plans. Click the line where his reasoning goes wrong." answer: 4 fault: logic misconception: fee-decides explain: "Line 4: Plan A's lower fee only wins up to 4 GB. After that its 5 dollars per GB adds up, and Plan B is cheaper. Which plan is cheaper depends on how much data you use." - check: type: question q: "The rule $T = 5g + 20$ gives $T = 10$ when $g = -2$. Why does that answer not make sense?" options: - "You cannot use negative data, so the rule only works for g of 0 or more" - "The rule is wrong: it should be T = 5g − 20" - "Phone plans can cost less than their fee" answer: 0 explain: "A model only fits the situation for some values. Data used cannot be negative, so the rule (and its line) starts at g = 0." ``` ### Comparing the plans Here is how to compare two plans and answer in words. ```worked T = 5g + 20, \quad T = 40 :: Plan A and Plan B, as rules. Which is cheaper, and when? 5g + 20 = 40 :: They cost the same where the two rules are equal: where the lines cross. g = 4, \; T = 40 :: The lines cross at $(4, 40)$. Check: $5 \times 4 + 20 = 40$. g < 4: \text{ A is cheaper} :: Left of the crossing, Plan A's line is lower. g > 4: \text{ B is cheaper} :: Right of the crossing, Plan B's line is lower. g \ge 0 :: The model only makes sense from 0 GB: you cannot use negative data. ``` Answer in words: "Up to 4 GB, Plan A is cheaper. At 4 GB they both cost 40 dollars. Above 4 GB, Plan B is cheaper." ### Find the mistake Read Leo's working one line at a time. Is his last line true for every amount of data? ### Does it make sense? Some values of $g$ make sense in the situation, and some do not. ## Modify: new comparisons ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: a plan with no fee, one amount catching up with another, two plans that never cross, and a model that stops working." try: { playground: board, starter: "graph.yml#gyms", height: 620 } tasks: - starter: "graph.yml#gyms" hint: "Gym A: 50 dollars to join, then 10 a week. Gym B: no joining fee, 15 a week. Follow both lines until they meet." check: { type: board, text: "Gym A is $T = 10w + 50$; Gym B is $T = 15w$. Drag $P$ to where they cost the same.", when: "P on y = 10x + 50 and P on y = 15x", explain: "At 10 weeks both cost 150 dollars. Before that Gym B is cheaper; after it, Gym A." } - starter: "graph.yml#savers" hint: "Sam starts with 30 dollars and saves 5 a week. Ana starts with nothing and saves 8 a week. When has Ana caught up?" check: { type: board, text: "Sam's savings are $S = 5w + 30$; Ana's are $S = 8w$. Drag $P$ to when they have the same amount.", when: "P on y = 5x + 30 and P on y = 8x", explain: "After 10 weeks both have 80 dollars. After that, Ana has more: her rate is bigger." } - starter: "graph.yml#parallel" check: type: question q: "Two electricians charge $T = 15h + 30$ and $T = 15h + 50$. When does the second one cost less?" options: ["Never: the lines are parallel, so the first is always 20 dollars cheaper", "After 2 hours", "After 4 hours"] answer: 0 explain: "Both charge 15 dollars an hour, so the lines are parallel and never cross. The first is always 20 dollars cheaper, for any job." - starter: "graph.yml#battery" check: type: question q: "A battery is modelled by $B = -10h + 100$. What does the model give after 12 hours, and does it make sense?" options: - "−20%: it does not make sense, so the model only works from 0 to 10 hours" - "−20%: the battery is 20% below empty" - "120%: the battery is overcharged" answer: 0 explain: "−10 × 12 + 100 = −20. A battery cannot go below 0%: it is flat at 10 hours, and the model stops there." ``` ### Gyms Each task puts a new pair of rules on the board. Drag $P$ to where they cost the same. ### Catching up Two people saving at different rates, from different starting amounts. ### Never crossing Two electricians with the same hourly rate. ### When the model stops A phone battery running down. ## Practise: compare and check ```step stage: practise insight: "Finding the crossing, choosing the cheaper plan for a given amount, and saying where a model makes sense, mixed; the review keeps writing rules fresh." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "Plan C costs 10 dollars plus 8 dollars per GB. Plan D costs 34 dollars for any amount. At how many GB do they cost the same?" answer: "3" feedback: - ["34", "34 is the cost where they meet. How many GB gives that cost on Plan C?"] - ["4", "Check: 10 + 8 × 4 = 42, not 34."] explain: "10 + 8g = 34, so 8g = 24 and g = 3. Check: 10 + 24 = 34." - check: type: question q: "Using Plans C and D, which is cheaper for 5 GB?" options: ["Plan D", "Plan C", "They cost the same"] answer: 0 explain: "Plan C: 10 + 8 × 5 = 50 dollars. Plan D: 34 dollars. Above 3 GB, D is cheaper." - check: type: question q: "Concert tickets cost $T = 12n + 6$ dollars for $n$ tickets. Which values of $n$ make sense?" options: ["Whole numbers from 1 up", "Any number, including 2.5", "Any number, including negatives"] answer: 0 explain: "You buy whole tickets, and at least one. The line joins the points, but only the whole numbers are real orders." - check: type: answer q: "Review: an electrician charges a 25 dollar call-out fee plus 9 dollars an hour. Write a rule for the total $T$ for $h$ hours." answer: "9h + 25" feedback: - ["25h + 9", "Which amount is paid once? That one is c."] explain: "T = 9h + 25: 9 dollars for each hour (m) and 25 dollars once (c)." ``` ### When they are equal ### Which is cheaper? ### Values that make sense ### Review ## Make: design a rival plan ```step stage: make insight: "Designing a plan that ties with Plan A at a chosen amount and beats it for heavy users reverses the lesson: from the crossing to the rule." try: { playground: board, starter: "graph.yml#make", height: 680 } hint: ["Plan A costs 50 dollars at 6 GB. Your line must pass through (6, 50).", "To be cheaper for heavy users, your rate m must be less than 5. Then choose c so 6m + c = 50."] check: { type: board, text: "Design Plan B so that it costs the same as Plan A at 6 GB, and is cheaper than Plan A above 6 GB.", when: "6m + c = 50 and m < 5", explain: "Your plan ties with Plan A at 6 GB (50 dollars) and has a lower rate, so it is cheaper for anyone who uses more." } ``` Plan A is $T = 5g + 20$. Set the rate ($m$) and fee ($c$) of your own plan. The green point shows where the two plans cost the same. Stretch: write an advert for your plan that is honest: who should choose it, and who should not? ## Make: gym or casual, on paper ```step stage: make insight: "The crossing says unlimited wins from 4 visits a month, but the model assumes steady visits; the judgement is whether the person really goes that often every month." hint: ["Write a rule for each plan: casual is 15 times the visits, unlimited is 55 whatever the visits.", "Where do they cost the same? Then look at the months Sam actually had."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A gym charges 15 dollars a visit, or 55 dollars a month for unlimited visits. Sam went 5, 4, 2 and 1 times in the last four months. On paper, find where the two plans cost the same, then decide which plan Sam should choose and why." steps: - ["Casual: $C = 15n$. Unlimited: $C = 55$", "write one rule for each plan, with $n$ the visits in a month"] - ["Same cost where $15n = 55$, so $n$ is about 3.7. Unlimited is only cheaper from 4 visits", "the lines cross between 3 and 4 visits"] - ["Sam's months cost 75, 60, 30 and 15 dollars casual: 180 in all, against 220 for four months of unlimited. Casual is cheaper, even though two months were over 4 visits", "the model assumes steady visits, and Sam's months are not steady"] picks: - step: 3 q: "Which is the best reason to choose casual for Sam?" options: - "Sam's quiet months mean unlimited costs more over the four months, even though busy months favour it" - "Casual always has the lower rate" - "The lines cross at 3.7 visits, so casual is always cheaper" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Casual costs more per visit than unlimited does once you go often. Which plan wins depends on the number of visits.", "The lines cross at 3.7 visits: casual is cheaper below that and unlimited above it."] criteria: - "I wrote a rule for each plan." - "I said where they cost the same, and which side each plan wins." - "I used Sam's real months, not just one month, to decide." explain: "The plans cost the same at about 3.7 visits a month. Sam's months were uneven: 180 dollars casual against 220 for unlimited, so casual is the better choice. If Sam went 4 or more times every month, unlimited would win." ``` Do this one in your book. The prices and Sam's visits are made up for the task, and a real gym may have joining fees or a minimum term. Write both rules, find where they meet, then choose the reason that decides it. **Also used in** - **Phone and streaming plans.** A lower fee with a higher rate beats a flat price only for light users. - **Hire and subscriptions.** Bikes, tools and software are all a per-use price against a flat one, and the answer depends on how often you use it. - **Breaking even.** A business asks the same question: from how many sales does the bigger fee pay off? ```teacher summary: Students put two linear rules on one graph, find where they are equal, decide which is cheaper on each side in the situation's words, and say where a model makes sense (AC9M8A03, node 2). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 12 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can find where two plans cost the same from their graphs, and say what that means. - I can decide which plan is cheaper for a given amount, and explain why in words. - I can say which values make sense for a model, and spot an answer that does not. struggle: "Choosing by the fee alone. Ask: work out both plans for a big amount and for a small one. Which is cheaper in each case?" before: > Do the Run and Modify boards yourself first. This lesson uses the last two: solving with graphs (where lines meet) and writing rules from situations. The new move is interpretation. The crossing answers "when are they the same?"; the lower line answers "which is cheaper?"; and every model has values where it makes sense (no negative data, whole tickets, a battery that stops at 0%). Answers should be sentences in the situation's words, not just numbers. The lines start at 0 on purpose: the graph itself shows where the model applies. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. 'Plan A, lower fee' is the common wrong answer. Ask a student who chose it to work out 6 GB on both plans." - "Run: once P is on the crossing, point left and right of it: which line is lower on each side?" - "Investigate: model the worked example live and finish with the sentence in words. Insist on the sentence: 'Up to 4 GB, Plan A is cheaper...'." - "Modify: before the electricians, ask: what did the c lesson say about lines with the same m?" - "Practise: for each answer, ask one student to say it as a sentence about the situation." - "Make: compare two students' rival plans. Both pass through (6, 50); which would you advertise to whom?" - "Paper: the gym task in Make is worked in books; the page marks the reason for the choice. Books out, then compare their three steps with the model." stuck: - see: A student says the plan with the lower fee is always cheaper (Leo's mistake). ask: Work out both plans for 10 GB. Which is cheaper now? fix: "The fee is only where the line starts. The rate decides who wins for large amounts: the lines cross, and the cheaper plan changes there." - see: A student gives the crossing as a number with no meaning. ask: What are the 4 and the 40 in this situation? fix: "Say it with units: '4 GB costs 40 dollars on either plan'." - see: A student accepts a negative or impossible answer. ask: Could this happen in real life? fix: List the values that make sense (0 or more GB, whole tickets, 0 to 100%) before answering. stretch: A third plan costs 25 dollars plus 3 per GB. Where does it cross Plan A and Plan B? Which plan is cheapest for 2, 5 and 10 GB? support: Give a table with g = 0 to 8 for both plans to fill in first; the crossing is where the two columns match. leads: > This finishes the Linear relations course so far. Later courses use the same ideas: simultaneous equations (two lines, one crossing, solved with algebra), inequalities (which side of a line), and non-linear models when a straight line stops fitting. Where it leads in class: any "which deal is better" question, break-even in business, and checking whether a model's answer makes sense in science. exit: q: Plan X costs 15 dollars plus 6 per GB; Plan Y costs 33 dollars flat. Which is cheaper for 2 GB and for 5 GB? Where do they cost the same? a: "2 GB: X (27 dollars vs 33). 5 GB: Y (45 vs 33). They cost the same at 3 GB (33 dollars)." explain: > To compare two plans, draw both rules on one graph. Where the lines **cross**, the plans cost the same. On each side of the crossing, the **lower line** is the cheaper plan. A plan with a lower fee is cheaper for small amounts, but a plan with a lower rate wins for large amounts. Always answer in words ("Up to 4 GB, Plan A is cheaper"), and check the answer makes sense: you cannot use negative data or buy half a ticket, so a model only fits some values. ```

# Graph boards for "Comparing two plans". Each plan is a line from 0 (you cannot use negative data or weeks).
# P is dragged to where the plans cost the same.

# region: run
widget: graph
axes: g (GB), T ($)
x: -0.5, 8
y: -2, 64
grid: off
snap: 1, 2
plot: y = 5x + 20, from 0
plot: y = 40, from 0
point P: 7, 6, drag
# endregion

# region: pic
widget: graph
axes: g (GB), T ($)
x: -0.5, 8
y: -2, 64
grid: off
plot: y = 5x + 20, from 0
plot: y = 40, from 0
cross: 1, 2
# endregion

# region: gyms
widget: graph
axes: w (weeks), T ($)
x: -0.5, 14
y: -5, 220
grid: off
snap: 1, 10
plot: y = 10x + 50, from 0
plot: y = 15x, from 0
point P: 2, 180, drag
# endregion

# region: savers
widget: graph
axes: w (weeks), S ($)
x: -0.5, 14
y: -5, 120
grid: off
snap: 1, 5
plot: y = 5x + 30, from 0
plot: y = 8x, from 0
point P: 12, 10, drag
# endregion

# region: parallel
widget: graph
axes: h (hours), T ($)
x: -0.5, 6
y: -5, 120
grid: off
plot: y = 15x + 30, from 0
plot: y = 15x + 50, from 0
# endregion

# region: battery
widget: graph
axes: h (hours), B (%)
x: -0.5, 14
y: -30, 110
grid: off
plot: y = -10x + 100
# endregion

# region: make
widget: graph
axes: g (GB), T ($)
x: -0.5, 10
y: -2, 80
grid: off
slider m: 0, 8, 6
slider c: 0, 60, 0, 2
plot: y = 5x + 20, from 0
plot: y = mx + c, from 0
cross: 1, 2
# endregion

# region: explain
widget: graph
axes: g (GB), T ($)
x: -0.5, 8
y: -2, 64
grid: off
slider k: 20, 50, 30, 10
plot: y = 5x + 20, from 0
plot: y = k, from 0
cross: 1, 2
# endregion

# region: leo
Plan A: 20 dollars a month plus 5 dollars per GB.
Plan B: 40 dollars a month, any amount of data.
Plan A has the lower monthly fee.
So Plan A is always the cheaper plan.
